Artifact 01
Stock Market Research Assistant
AI Chatbot · Conversational Agent
Introduction

As AI becomes central to financial technology, the ability to build accessible, intelligent tools for everyday users is a critical skill. This project explores how large language models can be applied to democratize stock market research — making complex financial data understandable to anyone, not just experts.

Description

A custom AI chatbot built on ChatGPT (GPT-4o) that allows users to ask natural language questions about stocks, sectors, and financial concepts. It delivers structured analysis — fundamentals, strengths, risks, and analyst sentiment — while staying within defined ethical boundaries: no personalized financial advice, no price predictions. Designed, prototyped, and tested using the full Design Thinking framework.

Objective

Help retail investors and students research stocks, compare investments, and understand financial data — through plain-English conversation, no financial expertise required.

Process
EmpathyMapped user pain points: financial data scattered across sites, jargon-heavy content, no affordable research tool for everyday investors.
DefineProblem statement: retail investors need a fast, conversational tool to explain stock fundamentals and trends in plain English.
IdeateEvaluated 4 approaches (live API bot, news aggregator, research assistant, portfolio tracker) — selected conversational assistant as highest feasibility.
PrototypeBuilt with ChatGPT's CustomGPT builder using a structured 10-question framework covering scope, tone, guardrails, and response format.
TestValidated across 7 scenarios. Iterated by adding mandatory risk disclosures, enforcing disclaimers on every analysis, and tuning temperature for consistency.
Test Scenarios Covered
Single stock analysis
Stock comparisons
Sector research
Financial term definitions
Out-of-scope handling
Follow-up context retention
Unknown ticker handling
Tools & Technologies Used
ChatGPT (GPT-4o) CustomGPT Builder NLP / LLM Design Thinking Prompt Engineering
Value Proposition
Unique Value

This project goes beyond using AI as a user — it demonstrates the ability to architect, scope, and constrain an AI system responsibly. Defining what the bot will and won't do, engineering guardrails into a conversational system, and validating behavior through structured test cases are skills most engineers don't yet practice.

Relevance

FinTech teams building intelligent, user-facing products need engineers who understand both the technical and ethical dimensions of AI. This artifact shows readiness to contribute to AI feature development — applicable to environments like Fidelity Investments where AI-forward platforms are actively being built. Others exploring conversational AI design can also use this as a reference for responsible scoping and iterative testing.

Artifact 02
100 Years of AI: A Visual Timeline
Presentation · Historical Research
Introduction

Artificial intelligence did not appear overnight. It emerged across decades of breakthroughs, setbacks, and paradigm shifts — shaped by a handful of visionary researchers and repeated cycles of hype and disappointment. Understanding this history is essential for anyone working in AI today.

Description

A 5-slide PowerPoint presentation tracing 100 years of AI history — from Alan Turing's 1939 Enigma work through the AI winters of the 1970s and 80s, the deep learning revolution, and the generative AI era. Each slide covers a distinct era with key milestones, figures, and context. The final slide presents a full visual arc with a timeline, key figures, and cited sources.

Objective

Synthesize 100 years of AI history into a clear, visually engaging presentation that helps audiences understand how we arrived at modern AI — and why each era matters.

Process
ResearchGathered primary sources including Our World in Data, IEEE Computer Society, and academic papers on compute trends across eras of machine learning.
StructureOrganized 100 years into four distinct eras: Founding Years (1939–69), AI Winters (1970–86), Deep Learning Revival (1986–2012), and the Generative AI Race (2015–present).
DesignBuilt each slide with a consistent visual language — era-specific color themes, milestone cards, and icon-driven layout — to make dense historical content scannable and engaging.
SynthesizeAdded analytical framing beyond raw facts: the AI winters slide explains why progress stalled (hardware limits, no data, missing algorithms) rather than just when.
CiteAll sources cited on the final slide with full attribution to original authors and publications.
Slides Covered
Founding Years (1939–69)
AI Winters (1970s–80s)
Deep Learning Revival
The AI Race (1986–Present)
Full Arc Timeline + Key Figures
Slideshow Preview
Slide 1 · Title — 100 Years of Innovation
Slide 2 · Era 1: Founding Years (1939–1969)
Slide 3 · The AI Winters (1970s & 1980s)
Slide 4 · Comeback + The AI Race (1986–Present)
Slide 5 · Full Arc Timeline & Key Figures
Tools & Technologies Used
Microsoft PowerPoint Data Visualization Research Synthesis Timeline Design
Value Proposition
Unique Value

This presentation goes beyond listing dates — it explains the why behind each era. The AI winters slide analyzes four structural reasons progress stalled (over-promised results, hardware limits, lack of data, missing algorithms) rather than treating the period as a simple pause. This analytical depth demonstrates the ability to contextualize technical history for any audience.

Relevance

For engineers and leaders working in AI today, historical context is a professional asset. Understanding how backpropagation ended the AI winter, how the Transformer architecture enabled LLMs, and how compute availability drove the current era makes it possible to reason more clearly about where AI is headed. This artifact demonstrates both communication skill and substantive AI literacy.

References

Roser, M. (2022). The brief history of artificial intelligence. Our World in Data. ourworldindata.org
Krishna Bhat, A. (2025, March). The evolution of AI. IEEE Computer Society. computer.org
Sevilla, J., et al. (2022). Compute trends across three eras of machine learning. arXiv.

Artifact 03
ML vs. Deep Learning: Real-World Analysis
Written Report · Comparative Analysis
Introduction

Choosing between traditional machine learning and deep learning is one of the most consequential decisions in AI system design. This report examines two real-world applications to show that the right technique is determined by the nature of the data, not by which approach is newer or more powerful in the abstract.

Description

A structured written report comparing traditional machine learning and deep learning through two real-world case studies: PayPal fraud detection (gradient boosting) and Google DeepMind retinal eye disease diagnosis (deep convolutional neural networks). For each case, the report explains why the chosen approach suits the problem and why the alternative would fail, covering data structure, feature engineering, interpretability requirements, and representational capacity.

Objective

Demonstrate the ability to select and justify the right machine learning approach for a given problem by analyzing the nature of the data, the constraints of the domain, and the technical limitations of each technique.

Process
ResearchIdentified real-world applications of both traditional ML and deep learning with publicly documented technical details.
AnalyzeExamined each problem's data characteristics: structured vs. unstructured, dimensionality, feature engineering feasibility, and regulatory context.
CompareFor each application, built a dual argument: why the chosen approach is appropriate and why the alternative would be unsuitable or would fail.
ReviseExpanded analysis based on instructor feedback to include deeper discussion of algorithm features, data nature, and more explicit suitability justification.
WriteOrganized findings into a professional report with section summaries, cited sources, and clear logical flow accessible to both technical and non-technical readers.
Case Studies Covered
PayPal fraud detection (ML)
DeepMind eye diagnosis (DL)
Structured vs. unstructured data
Interpretability requirements
Feature engineering limits
Regulatory constraints in AI
Tools & Technologies Used
Gradient Boosting / XGBoost Convolutional Neural Networks Microsoft Word Academic Research
Value Proposition
Unique Value

Most discussions of ML vs. deep learning stay at the surface level. This report goes deeper, analyzing why interpretability is non-negotiable in regulated financial systems, why volumetric medical images cannot be reduced to tabular features, and what representational capacity actually means when a traditional model hits its ceiling.

Relevance

Engineers who can articulate not just what AI technique to use but why, and why the alternative would fail, are significantly more effective on cross-functional teams. This skill applies directly to AI product decisions, architecture reviews, and stakeholder conversations where technical tradeoffs need to be communicated clearly.

References

Carey, S. (2021). How PayPal uses AI and machine learning to fight fraud. ComputerWeekly.

LeCun, Y., Bengio, Y., & Hinton, G. (2015). Deep learning. Nature, 521, 436-444.
Mitchell, T. M. (1997). Machine learning. McGraw-Hill.

Artifact 05
AI Ethics: The Ibrahim Diallo Case
Critical Thinking Analysis · AI Ethics
Introduction

As AI and automation take on greater roles in consequential decisions — hiring, firing, lending, healthcare — the ethical frameworks governing those systems matter as much as the technology itself. The Ibrahim Diallo case is a striking example of what happens when automation is deployed without human safeguards, and it raises questions every engineer building such systems should be able to answer.

Description

A structured critical thinking assignment analyzing the case of Ibrahim Diallo, a software developer whose automated HR system wrongfully terminated him after a manager failed to renew his contract in the system. The assignment identifies three core ethical issues — lack of human override capability, absence of transparency and communication, and an accountability gap — and proposes concrete solutions for each, grounded in ethical principles for responsible AI system design.

Objective

Apply critical thinking and AI ethics frameworks to a real-world case of automated decision-making gone wrong — identifying systemic failures, examining underlying assumptions, and proposing practical safeguards that center human dignity and accountability.

Process
SelectChose the Ibrahim Diallo case for its clear illustration of how rigid automation without human oversight can cause real harm — even without any malicious intent.
AnalyzeIdentified three distinct ethical failures: no override capability for senior managers, no notification or explanation to the affected employee, and diffused accountability with no named responsible party.
ChallengeQuestioned initial assumptions — shifting from "the manager should have fixed it" to recognizing the deeper design flaw: the system was built with no mechanism for human correction at all.
ProposeDeveloped concrete solutions for each issue: a two-manager approval step with a 48-hour review window, plain-language notifications with a human point of contact, and mandatory audit trails linked to a named accountability owner.
ReflectSynthesized the analysis into a personal framework: before building any system that affects people, ask — Can a human override this? Is the person affected informed? And is someone clearly accountable?
Ethical Issues Examined
No human override capability
No notification to employee
Accountability gap
Automation without safeguards
Design vs. implementation failure
Responsible AI deployment
Tools & Technologies Used
Critical Thinking Frameworks AI Ethics Analysis Case Study Method Microsoft Word
Value Proposition
Unique Value

This analysis goes beyond labeling the Diallo case as a system error. It traces each failure back to a deliberate design choice and argues that the absence of override capability, transparency, and accountability are not oversights but ethical violations baked into how the system was architected. That framing shifts the question from what went wrong to who is responsible for building it this way — which is the more important question for anyone building AI systems today.

Relevance

Engineers who build systems that affect people's lives — employment, credit, healthcare, access — carry an ethical responsibility that goes beyond making the code work. This artifact demonstrates the ability to think critically about that responsibility and articulate concrete safeguards, a skill that is increasingly expected in enterprise AI roles and essential for leading teams building consequential software.

References

Diallo, I. The machine fired me. idiallo.com
AI Incident Database. Incident #35. incidentdatabase.ai
The Register (2018). Software engineer fired, shut out of office for three weeks by machine. theregister.com
The Conversation (2018). This man was fired by a computer — real AI could have saved him. theconversation.com
